It's definitely frustrating losing all the progress on a large download. 

It happened to me too while pulling a image, and wondering if there's a solution to it because imo resuming a partially downloaded blob exactly where it left off is complex and not a standard behavior in most container runtimes yet.

No it is not difficult, this problem exists for probably decades and has already been solved in other applications. Maybe use/analyse wget??? Afaik it has a continue option. This is also a huge resource waste.

And the other thing I would reconsider is this 3GB layer, I assume this is cuda/gpu stuff, you do not need to download that all the time. I can't really imagine you have code changes of 3GB. So use layers more efficiently.

Oh yes sorry, also mentioned this at ollama. They need to fix their layers probably. 

Just pull any big container and while it is downloading pull your internet connection and then reconnect, you will notice that it starts downloading from 0. Actually you should be able to deduct this from what I posted, you can see the same image layer with different completed states.
@mtrmac can you remind us of the behavior of this type of thing? is it a full restart or do the completed layers get saved?

What I see in the original comment is that the user is pressing Ctrl-C. I don’t think it makes _any_ sense to “optimize” for that, by taking up gigabytes of disk space just on the chance that the user will run the same pull again.

On the first `storing blob to file …: happened during read: read …: connection timed out`:

---

The expected behavior is:
- Any unrecoverable error terminates the whole process; there might be locks held etc. but we don’t explicitly wait to finish anything that potentially could be finished.
- Layers which are completely downloaded, are committed on the fly, _in the layer order_ , and remain in storage if that happens before the process termination. So if the first layer is downloaded+committed, it will stay in c/storage, will not be re-downloaded on a future pull; but wastes on-disk space if a future pull never comes, and users must prune manually.
- Layers which are not completely downloaded, or layers which can not be committed yet, are, on process termination, discarded and must be downloaded from scratch again.
- If we see _specific kinds_ of network errors during layer download, not too frequently, and the registry supports range requests, the layer download will re-connect and resume. This works only within the one pull run, not across Ctrl-C; and involves heuristics that can, in principle, be fiddled with. (But I’m very uninterested in outright _removing_ them, causing an infinite retry loop on running out of disk space or I/O errors or the registry going permanently down.)  Any discussion of these heuristics would need a _precise_ output (notably including `heuristic tuning data` in the error message, if any, and ideally a `--log-level=debug` output). Ctrl-C is out of scope of these heuristics and not relevant.
- The top-level `--retry-times` is also a restrictive heuristic, but not _quite so_ restrictive. But, in that case, it behaves as if in the “Any unrecoverable error terminates the whole process” case; downloads within the same running process but across different retry attempts don’t share state, except for committed layers.

---

The “re-connect during layer download” heuristic seems not to be handling timeouts at all. That might be an easy thing to add.

_In principle_, it seems reasonable that with `--retry-times`, the process should be able to somehow keep state across the two different downloads and reuse the previous temporary files. The way it is implemented, this would be pretty non-trivial (and/or extremely ugly special-casing) to implement — and, again, it might not be always _wanted_ (what if the reason we are retrying is “the downloaded data does not match the expected digest”?).

Or, _purely hypothetically_, we could have a c/storage state of “pulling”, explicitly modeled, with c/storage “owning” the compressed binary files, as an explicitly tracked state. We’d then again _have_ to worry about pruning that data: currently users who just run `podman pull` and `podman rmi` never need to run `podman image prune` — only users who build containers do. If we had a persistent “pulling” state, that would change.

I mark this as feature because as described this works as intended currently. I think there is definitely something to be improved but I don't think that is particular critical either.

As noted this requires keeping track of the state. Maybe something that could be consider for the new storage design cc @mheon

(Right now the in-progress blobs are temporary state in c/image, not visible in storage anywhere. We _could_ make them c/storage-owned, under some kind of blob ID, and that could also be useful for the far-more-useful feature of not downloading the same layer several times on a concurrent start of many similar images. That’s also an example where freezing a plug-in API would be a limitation.)
